title: At the sea (Exodus 14)
hook: the army behind, water ahead; midrash says Nachshon walked in first

segments.voice: Yesterday, matzah: dough on their shoulders, a mixed multitude, and no time to wait. Your line was go when it's time. Did you send the flat bread? Now they're out, and trapped. Day eighty-nine.

Freedom lasts about three days before Pharaoh changes his mind. Again. He gets his chariots, six hundred of the best, and chases them. And the Israelites are camped by the sea. They look up and see the Egyptian army coming. Water in front. Soldiers behind. Nowhere to go. And the people panic, and turn on Moses with one of the most bitter lines in the Torah: "Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness?" Today: the moment between the army and the sea.
screen: `SIX HUNDRED CHARIOTS.` → `WATER AHEAD, SOLDIERS BEHIND.` → `WERE THERE NO GRAVES IN EGYPT?`

segments.voice: Moses answers with calm, famous words: "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD." Stand still. It sounds perfect. And then God says something surprising back to Moses: "Wherefore criest thou unto Me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward." Why are you crying out to me? Tell them to move. Go forward. Into the water? The Torah goes on: Moses lifts his staff, a strong east wind blows all night, the sea splits, "and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left." But the rabbis noticed a gap between go forward and the sea splitting. Who moved first? The Talmud tells a story. The tribes stood at the edge, each saying: I'm not going in first. You go. And then one man, Nachshon, son of Amminadav, a prince of the tribe of Judah, walked into the sea. Up to his ankles. His knees. His waist. His neck. The midrash says the water reached his nostrils, and only then did the sea split. There's another opinion in the same passage, that the tribe of Benjamin jumped in first. The Torah itself names no one. But the story of Nachshon stuck, so much that in modern Hebrew a nachshon is someone who goes first, a pioneer. The sea splits. The Israelites walk through on dry ground. The Egyptians follow, and the waters come back over them. The Torah says the people saw, and they believed. But first somebody had to get their feet wet.
screen: `STAND STILL, AND SEE.` · `SPEAK TO THEM, THAT THEY GO FORWARD.` · `NACHSHON WALKS IN.` · `A WALL ON THE RIGHT AND THE LEFT.` · then, large: `WALK IN FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take the first step before it's easy. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're standing at the edge of. A hard conversation, an application, a doctor's appointment, a new start. Notice that part of you is waiting for the sea to split first. For the fear to go, for a sign, for someone else to go. Now imagine the first step, just ankle deep. What is it, exactly? Picture yourself taking it. The bell holds the time.
At the sea. Trapped between an army and the water, the people are told go forward, and the midrash says Nachshon walked in first.
Your line: walk in first. Today, take the first small step into the thing you've been standing at the edge of. Day eighty-nine.

screen: `DAY 89 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SONG OF THE SEA.`

howItsDone: The crossing of the sea is read in synagogue on the seventh day of Passover, the day tradition says it happened, and on the Shabbat of the Song; Nachshon's story is a favorite in Jewish teaching about courage.

options: wait for the sea to split.

original.note: Hebrew: Nachshon, prince of Judah. in modern Hebrew, a pioneer, one who goes first.

trapdoor: what you thought: the sea split, and then they walked through.
what it means: the rabbis say someone had to walk in first, before it split.
what a scholar hears: Sotah 36b–37a: Rabbi Judah says Nachshon went first; Rabbi Meir says Benjamin. and yam suf is literally the sea of reeds.

notes: Sotah 36b–37a: Rabbi Meir (Benjamin first) and Rabbi Judah (Nachshon/Judah first). The detail 'water reached his nostrils' is from the Talmud citing Psalm 69:2 and later midrash (Mekhilta). Confirm.
'About three days': the text implies Pharaoh's pursuit after the people turn back (14:2–5); the three-day figure is traditional (Rashi on 14:5). Confirm.
Seventh day of Passover as the traditional date of the crossing: confirm.
